PROPOSED ADOPTION OF "o CANADA" IN BOTH ENGLISH AND FRENCH VERSIONS
The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Cote (Matapedia-Matane):
That, in the opinion of this house, the anthem "O Canada," in both the English and the French versions, should be the national anthem of this country.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to discuss the resolution, I want to join with the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) in congratulating the hon. member who moved the resolution. I also want to say that I think it is fitting that on occasion the house should consider a matter of this description which affects Canada in its growing sense of nationhood. There are two

National Anthem
kinds of sentiment as to nationhood, one that is good and one that is evil. The evil type of excessive and exaggerated nationhood is that which places one's own nationality above all others, and despises those who are of other nationalities. The good kind is the one in which the individual has a pride in the country in which he lives, and in the people of whom he is a part, but recognizes the good in others too.
I like to think that in our country we have grown to realize step by step that other nations have a contribution to make in the realm of international relations, and in the development of human society in all parts of the world, and that with otir diverse cultures we can work with them in developing the kind of world society of which we can be proud. We may well recognize the value of other beliefs and other cultures, and appreciate the distinctive attributes of different peoples as a contribution to the common welfare of mankind. I believe it is befitting that we in this country, with the consciousness of our distinctive nationhood in the world of nations, should have some symbols of nationhood.
I believe that in the adoption of a national song for Canada we are doing what almost every other nation has done in the past. May I recount a personal incident which emphasized the view that I then held, because we of this party are not recent converts to the idea that Canada should stand on her own feet. In company with my friend the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright), my friend the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), and indeed my friend the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. Probe), because he was there at the time in uniform, I remember that we had the great privilege of flying to Brussels in September, 1944, shortly after the Canadian troops reached that city. We found that the whole of the left flank of the allied armies along the coast of France and Belgium was under the control of the Canadian troops.
When we arrived in Brussels we were met and kindly received by a gentleman who is a citizen of Ottawa. I am sure he will not mind my mentioning this incident because I was reminded of it last month when I met him again. I refer to Brigadier Beament. He told us of an incident that I think emphasizes the suggestion that is now before the house. When our troops arrived in Brussels the people of Brussels not only welcomed them enthusiastically but set out to provide entertainment for them. Part of that entertainment was an opera. On the Saturday night previous to the day when we were there, the Canadian troops had attended an opera for the first time in the very fine opera house in Brussels. The people of Brussels wanted to honour the Cana-
[Mr. Coldwell.l
dian troops but they did not know what to play as the anthem of Canada. When they were informed that we had a certain song in Canada, which had become universally accepted in our country as the national anthem of Canada, no one could produce the music for it. I remember that Brigadier Beament told us how he had sent a special message to our high commissioner in London asking that a copy of "O Canada" and its music should be flown to Brussels so that it could be used on the following Saturday evening in the opera house in honour of the Canadian troops.
I recount that incident because it emphasizes the need for Canada-and I think now-to adopt a song that is acceptable to all the people of our country. Perhaps I might interject that I think the same thing about a Canadian flag. On that trip I also saw Canadian troops without a flag, but all the way along they had nailed, on the signposts and so on, pictures of the maple leaf, indicating that the Canadian troops were there. Over there you saw the flag of every other country except Canada; you heard every other song except the song of Canada. I do not think that is fitting for the nation that is Canada today.
There are some people who say that in making a statement of this description one is being disloyal to old symbols that we have had so long. I do not think that is so. I believe it would be well if we all recognized "God Save the King" as the symbol of our commonwealth association in which we are bound together by a common loyalty to a common crown. In that common loyalty to a common crown the valuable thing is the loyalty to a common symbol of unity among those great nations that comprise the commonwealth of nations. In the same way, I think it applies to a Canadian flag.
May I once more recount a personal experience? Last autumn when I had the privilege of again being in Great Britain, the country in which I was born, I noted when driving through the English countryside that over many of the public buildings the Union Jack was not flying but the cross of St. George. This is the red Latin cross on the white background, the flag of old England. If England flies a distinctive flag as well as the Union Jack, there is no reason why Canada should not have her symbol which she could fly with the Union Jack. I say there is no conflict between those of us who wish to preserve the sentiment of the commonwealth and those of us who wish to have a recognition of this nation which is Canada by the use of a symbol that is recognized as Canadian by all the nations of the world.
I do not want to speak at any length, but I do want to say this to my hon. friend who has moved the resolution, that I think the

tune of "O Canada" is now almost universally accepted from one end of this country to the other as the tune of our national anthem. About the words, I am not so sure. I know that I often address public meetings in various parts of Canada. At those public meetings we in this group make it a practice to open the meeting with the singing of "O Canada", and to close with "God Save the King". When "O Canada" is sung, I listen to the audience and I find that no common wording is used in it. Some sing "Glorious and free", and some sing "On guard for thee". I never know what any group of people will sing. If we are going to have a national hymn we must have the words set to our national tune so that words and tune are acceptable to all of us and can be used universally.
I do not think that in any way conflicts with the idea that was put forward by the member for Peel (Mr. Graydon).
What idea?
The idea that we should not try to bring about too much, shall I use the word regimentation, in this regard-
Rigidity.

That is a better word, and I thank my hon. friend for giving it to me. There is no desire on the part of anyone to make the thing so rigid it will be offensive, but I think there is a common desire on the part of all of us that in this country we shall achieve national unity. Unity in diversity it must be in some respects, but a unity of loyalty to our country; a unity of fellowship in which we can join together from time to time whether we speak French or whether we speak English, whether we speak Ukrainian or whether we speak Welsh. I may say that you could not tell a Welshman that "God Save the King", is the national anthem of Wales. He would tell you it was "Mae hen wlad fy nhadau", or "Land of Our Fathers".
I should say there should be no attempt to prevent each and every one of our people from singing the songs of their own land, but we should be able to join together in singing one song to indicate that we have a common Canadian citizenship, a common loyalty to a common country.

Mr. Speaker, I do not think I shall occupy very much time in speaking on this motion. The hon. gentleman who introduced it forgets one thing, namely, that all these matters of a new flag, a new anthem, a new governor general, and a bill to abolish appeals to the privy council, are only secondary matters and should not be raised at this time. I am not speaking for the official opposition but as one who has had
National Anthem
a great deal of admiration for the people of that great province of Quebec. I never forget what they did in France during the last war. Sixty thousand of our own troops from Toronto district went overseas, including some of the present ministers and the members on this side of the house. I plead with these members to forget these unimportant questions at the present time and to consider the unrest there is in the world. All members should consider that most important matter which the Prime Minister introduced on Monday. It was emphasized there was a need for security. We do not know actually to whom the country is going to belong; we face a very grave invasion threat by land, sea and in the air. I do urge my hon. friends from Quebec to consider security.
As I say, many of our soldiers from Toronto fell during the last war. They are buried in France, Belgium and the other countries over there. I am sorry that the hon. member has urged us to give consideration to this matter at the present time. I do not say that in any way to reflect upon the hon. member who moved this motion. I believe this same member last year introduced a similar motion in which he wanted to substitute the word "Canada" for the words "Dominion of Canada" in the Holiday Act. I believe it was Bill No. 8. I am not speaking for the official opposition. Since I have come into the house I have always endeavoured to support principles. All along, those principles have been clear-cut. I have not been one of those who are here today and away tomorrow. I have not changed my colours every five minutes nor have I worn a coat of many colours. I have persistently brought before the house national measures that would benefit all the people of this country and the working classes but many of them have been forgotten.
When you look at the history of this country from the time before confederation, you will see that it was the policy of men like Howe, Macdonald, Cartier, George Brown, all those great men, to live in a spirit of harmony. On many occasions tribute has been paid to what the French people have done to bind Canada together. Away back in 1844 Sir John A. Macdonald said we should be bound up with the mother country for all time. I believe it was Sir Etienne Tache who said that when it came to the defence of Canada the last shot would be fired by a French Canadian. That great Prime Minister, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, led the procession in the diamond jubilee of the empress queen, Queen Victoria. Men of all races, from all over the world, flocked to the glorious diamond jubilee in 1897 of the late empress queen. They came from cape, island and continent.

National Anthem
Men of forty or fifty different races jostled each other in the streets of London, the metropolis. Kipling wrote then that great hymn, The Recessional. We are in recessional days now so far as the British empire is concerned. India has gone. Burma has gone. They have all passed away and the days of The Recessional are upon this country at the present moment. I am sorry that those from our sister provinces cannot see these things in the same way as I do.
At the diamond jubilee Sir Wilfrid Laurier, who was first in the procession because we were the senior dominion, said: If you want our support, invite us to your councils. This they did. We have always been at those councils. The great Liberal Prime Minister also stated that when Britain is at war, Canada is at war. I am not one of those who are turncoats. I have never been a turncoat. I believe in speaking the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. The people back in the constituencies cannot get the truth or the full truth, but only the official truth from some of the newspapers, the radio or the Canadian press. They do not give the people back home the truth. They give them only as much of the truth as they want them to know, forgetting that there are large numbers of people back in the constituencies who know as much as or more than some of the agencies I have named. I am not complaining about the matter at all. I just refer to that point in order to see how some of them change their policy or their tune accordingly.
As to this motion, I will just say that I greatly regret this purely secondary matter has been brought up at the present time, because there are many other matters which are far more important than it is. Last year we had a motion, proposed by the mover of this motion, that there should be a change from the Dominion Day Act to Canada Act. Then there was a resolution to change the flag. We had a committee on the flag. So many flags were submitted, I never saw the like of it in my life. There were all kinds. They were green, pink, grey-all the colours of the rainbow. A committee investigated the flag situation. What did they do? Their report was presented to the house and it was forgotten in the twinkling of an eye.
Another resolution proposed to change Dominion day to Canada day, and still another to abolish appeals to the privy council. The Minister of Justice is not here to hear the discussion; but many eminent men who have occupied that great office, such as Sir Charles Fitzpatrick and Sir Allen Aylesworth and many others, have been opposed to any change with regard to appeals to the privy council; because, if you believe

them, it is the one court in which a litigant can get justice. Another motion proposed here is to change the office of governor general-to have a Canadian governor general. We have had two of the greatest soldiers in the history of the world, Montgomery and Lord Alexander, the present governor general. They are men who have never been excelled. It is about time we named a mountain after the two of them, commemorating accordingly those who have fought for the country. They are also great statesmen and front-rank diplomatists as well.
There are several other matters which I might mention but I will not take up the time of the house to do so. I will just say this. Since coming into the house I have supported certain principles because I believed it was far better for us to tell the people the truth. You will notice that there is an exit now of large numbers of those people with the halos up there; gentlemen in what one of them called the hayloft, in a jocular way. Hardly any of them are here to hear the discussions after the orders of the day are called.
I want to refer just for a moment to the substance of the motion; which reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, the anthem "O Canada", in both the English and the French versions, should be the national anthem of this country.
I want to point out to the house right now that the anthem "God Save the King" is a prayer. It is both a prayer and an anthem. It is quoted at the coronation. It is a prayer for the safety of His Majesty. Before the war started, Their Majesties visited Canada. Did they ever get a better reception anywhere than they got in Canada? I do not think so. In the province of Quebec, which they visited, they were accorded a glorious reception, as they were in all the provinces. So much was that so that the present queen, when she returned to England, said that it was like a second coronation to have had the glorious reception that the people gave them in every part of Canada. In no part of Canada was a better reception given to Their Majesties than at Riviere du Loup and many other places at which they stopped in the province of Quebec. That just shows how well thought of Their Majesties are in this country.
As I say, "God Save the King" is founded on the bible, I Samuel, chapter 10, verse 24. After all, we are a Christian country, or we are supposed to be. We have many Christian churches and they are working in the utmost harmony. We saw that fact exemplified in the Indian and Eskimo affairs committee. The heads of these great Christian churches,

Protestant and Catholic, came before the committee and made recommendations. I hope we shall never see racial and religious jealousies raised in this parliament, because we are a people united from coast to coast as a Christian nation.
I believe that the Prime Minister brought before the house last Monday, in clear-cut phraseology, the main problem, as did the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) on this side of the house and the leaders of the other groups. They showed the people of Canada what is the most important duty of the hour, namely, the Atlantic pact, to bind ourselves together in order to ensure security.
As to this resolution, I do not intend to say anything against the proposal myself, because "O Canada" is not a prayer and it is not an anthem. It forgets all about the Lord, creation and Christianity. I may say that there are many versions of "O Canada". They ignore the king and queen; they ignore the coronation oath; they forget everything. Why are all these matters, which are only secondary, being raised, with the enemy right at the door of the St. Lawrence where we have no real security or defence? The other day we heard that five hundred divisions are all ready for the east against the west. Why are we raising all these troublesome secondary questions? They are not raised in New Zealand, in Australia, or in any of the other dominions. Why are they brought forward at the present time? That is the question I ask. They are only secondary. They are not needed at the present time. Why can they not wait and be brought up after security is assured? Today we have no security. There was a submarine right up at Riviere du Loup. In 1947 I was down in Riviere du Loup for the first time in my life, and down through the eastern townships. I had never before been down to the south shore.
I saw the cove at Riviere du Loup where the enemy submarines came up the river. I was in the house occupied by Sir John A. Macdonald in Riviere du Loup for twenty-seven summers. A private session of the house was called here in 1943. At that private session the minister of naval affairs, the Hon. Angus Macdonald, who is now the able premier of Nova Scotia, told us about the grave danger the country was in. At the present time the gravity is ten times as great. We have not one up-to-date submarine. We are depending on the United States for defence. They are spending billions of dollars- on what? They are spending billions of dollars on defence because the next war, when it comes, will be far worse than the last one. At the present time we have only a Carthaginian peace with Russia. We did something the other day when we passed the
National Anthem
Atlantic pact. It was passed to bring about a spirit of unity, liberty and freedom, binding us together with the great nation to the south of us which has done so much in two wars to support the people of this country and to try to give security. They will be remembered in the years to come for what they have done.
I may say that we are forgetting all about these things. There will be two agencies in the next war. Britain and the dominions are facing very grave times. The dangers will come from the air, because the head of the air force in Britain told the House of Commons about it the other day. I am sorry I cannot refer very much to it today. He told Britain to beware. They have to beware because they may be destroyed by the air force which Russia has at the present time.
The second grave danger is submarine war. The war will be under the sea. We have no modern submarines. We are depending on the United States. As was said the other day in the old country, part of the defence lies under the sea. Today the United States has supremacy in submarines which can stay underneath the water for six months or a year. They are costing billions of dollars. We have to thank the people of the United States for what they are doing for us in submarine warfare to make secure the North American continent, and Canada is helping in the radar screen in the Arctic.
At the present time there is no necessity of bringing these secondary matters forward. Another thing which the hon. member might have explained is this. There are many versions of "O Canada". They forget all about the divinity. I am sorry that these matters have been brought up at the present time. I have supported certain principles ever since I have been a member of this House of Commons, and I have not been ashamed to do so. The time is coming when we shall find that we have no real security whatever and there is no use pretending we have. All these plans such as the security pact, the UNO and various leagues of nations we have had in the past. I call all these matters separatism and isolation. Do not forget that a million men went from the dominions in the first war. They went over there not to fight for Britain but to be at her side and to support her in the great war. One hundred and thirty-five thousand of these men fell on the field of battle and they are buried in Flanders and in France and in many parts of the world. They changed the whole history of the world. Are we going to forget all about these men who are buried over there? If our status, our autonomy and our sovereignty were good enough for these men who are buried in France and Flanders today it should be good

National Anthem
enough for those who stayed at home. That is one of the points I wish to make.
I do not believe that these matters should be discussed at the present time, Mr. Speaker. I am not going to occupy any more of the time of the house. We owe a great deal to the French people. France will always be a great nation. Edward VII loved the French people. What would we have done in the first war if it had not been for them? We would have lost the war. Look at the way they suffered in the first war. In the United States a bomb was not thrown or a farm destroyed. They had the security of the British fleet-the real Monroe doctrine.
What was the Monroe doctrine? It was the supremacy of the seas by Britain for four centuries, from the days of Philip of Spain, Louis XIV, Napoleon and so on. The Monroe doctrine was all very well. What was the Holy Alliance? It was an alliance between Russia, Prussia, and Austria, the same powers that are against us today. What was the result? We had that Holy Alliance from 1815 to 1823. It led to the United States adopting the Monroe doctrine. What was it? It was simply the protection of the British fleet and the supremacy of the seas. That is what it was. We have lost it today. It has been expanded to include the whole Atlantic on both sides now, the same Monroe doctrine against the very same people of Russia, Prussia and Austria, by the grace of the United States and President F. D. Roosevelt.
I ask the house to consider these things in the light in which I have given them. I have been a great admirer of the French people and what they did for this country in the past.
I believe their leaders were magnificent. We have never had such leaders as they had before and after confederation. If we want real security let us forget all these secondary matters, and let us unite as a people from coast to coast, because we do not know what real military security we have today. We have only eleven and a half million people. We may be in grave danger. Therefore I urge the house to forget all about these secondary questions until a more opportune time arrives. For these reasons, Mr. Speaker,
I should like to see the motion withdrawn until we get some reasonable security.

I am
quite ready to congratulate the mover of the resolution on having the courage of his convictions, and on having placed his convictions in the form of the resolution before the house; but I must say that I am very much disappointed in the contributions which have been made in the debate by the two speakers who officially represented the two other

groups in the house. It is my view that in this critical time of history the bond of unity between the British commonwealth of nations should be strengthened rather than weakened. May I ask, what is the hurry in regard to this matter? Why must we proceed with this matter during this session? There are many matters of national and international importance which could well occupy the time of this house for the days remaining not only before Easter but throughout the entire session. What about such problems as the marketing of our farm produce in the future? What about the threatening international situation? What about such matters as the discriminatory freight rate structure, which this government continues to support and allows to exist from year to year? I could name a score of other problems which require the immediate attention of the house. And whether it is this government or a government formed by some other party which will sit on the government benches after the next election, the fact remains that that government will be faced with these same unsolved problems. It is about time we did something about them.
Let me remind the house once again that we are living in one of the most critical stages of history. Yet, here we are discussing something which is dividing us, whereas we need unity at this particular time. Whatever may be the views held on this matter in various sections of Canada, I believe this is not the time to bring such contentious subjects before the House of Commons. I think no one will accuse me of favouring one side or the other, or of being prejudiced in favour of the opinions held by French Canadians or Canadians of Anglo-Saxon origin. I am neither of Anglo-Saxon nor of French-Canadian origin, and for that reason I am sure no one will accuse me of being prejudiced in this instance.
I do say however that never in my life did I feel prouder or happier than when, on the occasion of touring Europe two years ago, I was able to present a Canadian passport bearing on it the words "British subject". I was proud of that.
The leader of the C.C.F. stated that this was one step toward the realization of the full stature of Canadian nationhood. Well,
I believe no one in Canada now is denied the privilege of singing "O Canada" as many times as he wishes. No one denies any Canadian that privilege in any part of Canada -and that is the way we should keep it.
Many Canadians of Anglo-Saxon origin do not, believe me, fully realize how fortunate they are in being able to say that "God Save the King" is their anthem, one which binds us together as members of the British com-

monwealth, and which stands as a symbol of the unity of the commonwealth-an organization which, to my mind, has never had its parallel in the history of the world. Yet we listen to members skating around the problem, afraid that it may be used as a political weapon in some by-election or in a general election. I say this matter is greater than a by-election or a general election, and we must realize that fact at once.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) said, further, that we should stand on our own feet. I agree with him on that point. But do we not stand on our own feet if we continue to have the right to choose between singing either "O Canada" or "God Save the King"? Surely no one denies us that right. Surely no one denies us the right to proceed toward the realization of full nationhood in Canada.
The hon. member also mentioned that it had been difficult on some occasions to obtain the music for "O Canada". Surely that is a weak argument for throwing "God Save the King" overboard. Surely we can obtain as many copies of "O Canada" as we like. One cannot find fault with "God Save the King" simply because there have been some Canadians who were not able to find the words and music for "O Canada".
They were in Europe.
They may have been in Europe; but it is up to Canadians to educate their children in such a way that they would know the words of "O Canada".
Canada has nothing to do with education in Belgium.
But still we have Canadian representatives there, and had our soldiers there.
"O Canada" was not official.

It does not matter. They
could have obtained the words of "O Canada".
Regardless of arguments which may be offered for or against the availability of music for "O Canada", I say this issue is greater than that of simply getting rid of "God Save the King." It goes deeper than that.
On the order paper there are resolutions dealing with various subjects; but the broad aim of some of them would seem to be identical, namely, to weaken the bonds between Canada and the other members of the commonwealth. I hear an hon. member applaud; but I say to him that if he would reflect for a moment upon the position of Canada he would realize that there is no such thing as an absolutely independent Canada. He would know that thirteen million people must depend upon one nation or another for
National Anthem
assistance in the event of crisis. He should realize also that if we broke away completely from the British commonwealth we, on this continent, would soon become a part of or be tied closer to our neighbour to the south. I realize that our relationships with that neighbour are satisfactory. We listen to their radio programs; we read their literature; we read their press; we hear their speakers, and in that way we have connection with our American friends. But we should also maintain close relationship with the United Kingdom, even if only for the one reason: that if in Europe today the United Kingdom were wiped out, Europe would fall under the control and into the hands of the U.S.S.R. There is no question about that. Do we want that result? Surely not. I say that our French-Canadian friends should think this matter through a little more carefully; they should go beyond the superficial and at times prejudicial attitude which they take on these matters.
I want to repeat that if the United Kingdom is weakened any more than she has been in recent years it will be some other nation, perhaps one unfriendly to our interests, that will dominate Europe. That would not be in the interests of Canada. That is the position I take and that is the position I have always taken.
Then again I wish to draw to your attention, and through you to the attention of hon. members, a strange coincidence in so far as some of the measures that have been placed on the order paper are concerned. On the one hand, the government is pushing through as quickly as possible measures which would bring about certain ties between the members of the British commonwealth of nations through certain pacts, even bringing in nations from outside the British commonwealth of nations; and, on the other hand, supporters of the government bring in other measures that undo what the government intends perhaps to do.
That is unfair.
It is not unfair.
It is.
It is true.
It is not true; it is unfair.

If hon. members will permit me to go ahead they will have an opportunity to reply. Here is what I had intended to say. We have voted for the resolution favouring the North Atlantic pact. What is the purpose of the North Atlantic pact? It is to bind together the British commonwealth of nations.

No.

National Anthem

Just a minute, be patient. At the same time it brings about the support of a few other nations in order that we may withstand any combination of hostile nations which may also join their forces together.
The hon. member has not read it.
Is it confined to the signatories?
Perhaps I should repeat what I said.
I should like to ask the hon. member a question.
Address the Chair.
I did address the Chair.
The hon. member was not looking in that direction.
Do not the terms of the North Atlantic pact relate to the signatory nations only? If that is true, is it not also true that only two nations of the commonwealth have signed it?
The hon. member is quite right in one sense but-
She has no sense.
I am not alone in that.

I do not recall whether it was the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) or the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) who stated that the ideas expressed in Mr. Churchill's speech at Fulton gave birth to the Atlantic pact.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The hon. member is wrong again.

One hon. member placed that on the record and I do not need to go very far to prove the point. When Mr. Churchill spoke at Fulton he said that this was the time for the members of the British commonwealth and the United States to get closer together. The nations that signed the North Atlantic pact went a step further and brought in a few other nations. But the purpose of the pact is exactly what Mr. Churchill had in mind and I do not think hon. members will disagree with that.
That is what the government is doing on the one hand. They are appealing to the Canadian people to support this pact, and we are supporting it. I really was proud of the way in which the debate was handled in this house and of the contributions which were made in that connection. The government was doing that on the one hand and then, on the other hand, these measures have been brought in to throw overboard every connection that we have ever had with the British commonwealth of nations. To my mind that 
is-I do not know just what to say-double talk or something of the sort. It certainly is not what we should be doing at this moment.
It is not in the bill either.

It surprises me to see or to hear hon. members taking this matter so lightly. As I pointed out, this is only one measure and there are others to follow. Where are we going to stop? Let me ask hon. members: will they tell me what disadvantages we suffer by co-operating with the United Kingdom?
That has nothing to do with it.
Hon. members are not going to decide what I am going to say.
You are beyond the question.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Is it in order?

I am speaking my own mind and what I believe, and hon. members may do likewise. As I have mentioned before, the world situation is critical, more critical than many of us realize, more critical than the official opinions which appear in the newspapers would indicate. We Canadians must get our thinking straight at this time. Many of us listen to radio programs and we hear attempts to compare the system existing in the Soviet union with that existing in Canada. One man plays the part of a Russian and he is asked the question: What are the advantages of your system? The answer is, "We are all equal in the Soviet union. There we have no rich men and no poor men. Everybody in Russia is nobody." That may appeal to a simple mind, and it may be a good joke; but, Mr. Speaker, it is wrong for us to underestimate the group of men who plotted in exile less than thirty-five years ago, and who are today in possession of more than half of Europe, and have infiltrated into the ranks of practically every country in the world. I say that the attitude of underestimating your opponent in this case is a bad one. That is not the attitude which Canadians should adopt. We should strive to improve our lot, and at the same time we should not adopt the philosophy that, simply because of certain changes that are suggested here and there, we should throw overboard those things for which the British people and others fought for centuries. We should not do that just because somebody brings up a slogan, "let us change it; let us have something new." A new style is all right when it comes to clothes and certain other things; but let me say to you that, in matters such as these, we should proceed slowly and carefully. I say with all sincerity

that not only Canadians of Anglo-Saxon origin but even those of French-Canadian origin will be proud that they have remained loyal to these principles, as they always have been. At the same time, they will not discard this symbol of unity, this symbol the equal of which no other group of nations in the world possesses.

Mr. Speaker, I have one or two suggestions to offer. First I should like to congratulate the hon. member who has brought the subject before the house in order that we may have a full dress debate on it. He is showing that he believes in his own province and he also believes in Canada. When I was a young fellow I chose Canada instead of New Zealand, Australia, Scotland, England, or any other place, because I felt that Canada was the country that would suit me. To me it is the greatest country on earth today. If you will think of those things that we have in Canada which demonstrate how we outshine any other country in the world you will be surprised. We have the longest railway in the world. We have the greatest fresh-water lake in the world. You could drop Ireland into that great lake-
Never.

-and all you would see would be the Guinness' stout sign. We have the greatest grain-growing country in the world, the greatest mines in the world, and the last war showed that we have the greatest men in the world. Because Canada is great I think we should have a flag, and I think we should have a national anthem. Like the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) I like the tune of "O Canada". When I came to this country first the people were singing "The Maple Leaf Forever". Then we were singing "O Canada". I remember once, when we were singing "O Canada, our home and native land", somebody was kind enough to say, "Dan, that shuts you out; Canada is not your home and native land".
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar cannot say that it is his native land unless he takes it the way the Irishman took it when he was talking about patriotism, that a man was loyal to his native land whether or not he was born there. I should like to make two suggestions. As I think of Canada today and what makes her great, it is what the Christian churches all over stand for. Without the teachings of the Christian churches Canada would go to the bowwows. I suggest that, as the outcome of this debate, a committee should be formed to study the question of a national anthem.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
That is what was done with the flag.
National Anthem
And instead of singing "our home and native land", let us put something in there that will include everybody.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The best way to kill a suggestion is to refer it to a committee.

When you sing "O Canada" today you cannot tell whether we are Christian or heathen. The heathen are loyal to their native lands too. We are loyal to our native land, but why leave God out. He is the foundation of our country, and if you leave Him out of our national anthem it will not represent people like myself.
We have it in the French version.

Therefore, in congratulating the hon. member who moved the resolution, I say to him that I think we should have a committee to study the question of a national anthem that will be worthy of the great name of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I cannot approach this subject as a musician. I am a musician of the barber shop variety, and that is all. Therefore I am unable to give you any opinion as to whether this, that, or the other is a good piece of music, but I have listened to six speakers today, and referring to the committee which the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) wants, my suggestion is that the six gentlemen who have spoken should form a sextet, and they will ruin any song that was ever written. I do not think there is any doubt of that.
I speak as one who was born in this country, as were my people before me. My grandparents on one side came from the same place as the hon. member for Fort William, if I do not mistake his accent, and I do not think I do. What I want to say is that in the place where I live, and in the larger area of that part of the country in which I live, "O Canada" is sung at the opening of all meetings. It is taught in our schools, and as far as the children are concerned, my children and now my grandchildren, I am inclined to think that they already regard this song or anthem-I do not know the proper name for it-as the national anthem. I say that most sincerely. I have come to the conclusion that the young men of my acquaintance who returned from this war regard "O Canada" as the national anthem of Canada. In other words I think, sir, that that sentiment is growing in Canada and growing in a very healthy way.
I put this to the house: of what advantage is it to pass a statute which will, in fact, put this song in a strait-jacket? Really, that is the only thing it will accomplish. With the

National Anthem
greatest respect, I say that if we leave things alone, let the development take its own natural course, the day will come when that will be regarded universally as the national anthem of this country. But remember, it will be one of two anthems. We commence all our school meetings, rotary clubs, service clubs and all those meetings with one of these songs and as the song is sung the people turn and face the flag.
I must say I was somewhat impressed by what the member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) said. He advanced the idea that the Deity should be mentioned in the national anthem of any country. If you go to the United States, you will find that they have two anthems, "My Country 'tis of Thee" and "The Star Spangled Banner". There is no statute covering the situation, but there are these two songs both of which are patriotic. On some occasions both of them are sung, and on all occasions one of them is sung. I am sure there must be in this House of Commons other members present beside myself who listen to the fights from Madison Square Garden every Friday night. On that occasion you will find that "The Star Spangled Banner" is sung before the opening of the fight. I have never been there, but I assume the people rise while that tribute to their country is paid in song by those who are present.
Let us consider the United Kingdom. So far as I know, and I think I am right in this, there is no statute covering "God Save the King." Take different parts of the United Kingdom-I was going to say, having regard to racial origin, but perhaps that is not a correct expression, because the Scotchmen claim that they populated Ireland and that the Irish are really Scotch. There is the Celtic part of the races in the United Kingdom which covers the Welsh, of course. We have heard something about their anthem, but again it is not an anthem put in a strait-jacket by legislation.
If this matter came to a vote at the moment, I have no idea how I should vote. I am in this position-
As usual.

I think that was at least an unkind remark that was made just now. Inasmuch as we are trying to be tolerant with each other, I will just leave it at that.
I will say this,, that I am very fond of the song. I must say that since the return from the war of my own son, who believes as many of us do that we should have something distinctively Canadian, I am influenced by that. The important thing at the moment, sir, is that there is a growing stream, and I believe legislation of this type will act as a dam to

that growing stream. I believe that if the natural forces are left to themselves, if it be left to the quiet judgment not only of members of parliament but of our own people and particularly those of different racial origins who mingled so closely in this last great war, we shall have done much more for unity in this Dominion of Canada. If a statute is passed now one has the feeling, which perhaps one cannot prove, that it will bring about disunity. Surely, a danger of that kind is something which should be appreciated. If we have nothing to gain by saying that we shall have one national anthem, because that is what the resolution means, then with the greatest respect to the mover of this motion, I suggest that we delay the matter.
I wish to compliment the member for Matapedia-Matane (Mr. Cote) on the courage he has shown in moving the resolution. I do say that nothing can be lost by a little delay and nothing can be gained by haste. With respect to all concerned, is it not the part of wisdom to let this thing grow in its natural way? In the event of some of us not being satisfied with the growth of that sentiment, then we could bring the matter up here. If we must, let us divide on it at that time. I am afraid that if we divide on the question now we may add to the ideas of some persons outside this house and outside the parties in this house, we may add fuel to the flame of their efforts in creating disunity in this Canada of ours which we all love so much.

Mr. Speaker, I think I am in accord with a great many of the thoughts expressed by the member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith). I believe it would be unfortunate if the house were to divide at this time on this particular question, and particularly in view of the stand we took last Monday. We are all working for the unity of Canada, and perhaps this is once when a question such as this should be given more serious thought than at any other time in the history of our country.
I quite appreciate that a reference to the debate when the report of the flag committee came before the house would not be entirely in order, but I believe it has a very close connection with this resolution. I think it is a good thing to have a resolution such as this brought before the house once in a while, in order that we may turn our attention to the matter in the hope it will bring about greater unity. That of course brings up the question as to whether this resolution, as it is framed at the present time, will bring about that result. If the hon. member, in framing his resolution, instead of using the words "the national anthem" had used the words "a national anthem", I think we could

have dealt with it from a different angle and could have taken a broader point of view with regard to the question. But 1 feel that Canada, to a greater extent than ever before, has been swept into the centre of the international scene and that she finds her problems are more and more those of the world at large. That fact was shown, as I said a moment ago, last Monday. We can pick up the papers any day and find that there is throughout the world unrest, to overcome which requires the co-operation of the peace-loving nations. We can bring about that fine co-operation of the peace-loving nations only if we are able to keep our own nation properly united.
Both geography and history have given to Canada a place of importance. It is true that in recent years we have come to the point at which we can say that Canada has attained to nationhood at a moment when the ground-swell of vast changes is felt throughout the world; and she will, if she follows her true intuition and interest, play a distinctive role in creating that community of nations whose existence is essential to any hope of ensuring international prosperity and peace. Because of that consideration of international good will, I question whether it is wise at this time to consider a motion such as this.
In dealing with this question from a national standpoint, we must face two questions. First, we must ask ourselves: Has Canada really arrived at the status of nationhood? Second, in dealing with national affairs from a national standpoint, I believe we must ask ourselves this question: What can Canada contribute to the creation of that world community of nations which we talked about when discussing the Atlantic pact last Monday? Those are important side issues of this important motion with which we are dealing. Because of those considerations I feel that the hon. member would have been well advised if, after having presented the motion in such an able manner, he had either withdrawn it or allowed it to stand until some future date. As I said a moment ago, Mr. Speaker, I feel that this is hardly the time to bring a question of this nature before this house.
I asked the question, Mr. Speaker, whether Canada had attained the status of nationhood. I think we should endeavour to answer that question. Of late years much has been written about our history, particularly about the province of Nova Scotia, from which I come. Some able writers down there have placed on the market outstanding books on the history of Nova Scotia. I refer particularly to that able contribution made by Thomas Raddall in his latest book, The Warden of the
National Anthem
North, dealing with Nova Scotia and more particularly with the city of Halifax. So, as I say, of recent years we have had books which have given us the great historical background of our own country and of our own province, about the men and women who pioneered this great country of ours. We learned of their bringing with them not only their material goods but their political opinions, their manner of living, their prejudices and ambitions, which they adapted to the demands of their new environment. May I pause here to say that this same thought applies to the large numbers of immigrants who entered our country last year and who are still weekly, or almost daily, entering this country in the first months of this year 1949. They are all bringing with them the same ideas as did the pioneers of the early days. They will fall into the pattern of our country, as did our forefathers; and they will make good citizens, good Canadians, and help to perpetuate the fine traditions of Canada.
Then again, Mr. Speaker, the geography and other circumstances of the Canadian scene modeled their feelings, interests and actions so as best to suit their needs and purposes. Across the years we all have helped to build out of our background the structure of this fine Canadian nation. Our present stage of Canadian political development, the parliamentary principle adopted from our mother country, Britain, is a distinctive admixture of British and American procedures. I do not think that we should try to break down any of those ties between the motherland and Canada. Those ties have been helpful to us over a long period of years. Because of that fact, I would hesitate at this time to introduce and bring into effect the results which would be attained if we were to adopt this motion.
Our national historical background and our geographical environment alike have, so far, largely determined the direction of Canada's development toward nationhood.
Just killing time.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order.

With a more united maritimes, and with added strength from the advent of Newfoundland, I believe it lies within our power, as thinking citizens, to guide our development to better advantage and to greater ends. And what I say about the eastern maritimes applies equally to the western sections of our country, particularly British Columbia. This is another reason why we should not today take definite action on this motion.
Canada's economic development has shown in the past the presence of intermingled forces running east-west and north-south, working

National Anthem
to some extent at cross purposes. I am now going to bring into this discussion, Mr. Speaker, a thought that might be considered for the moment to be out of order; but I sincerely trust that you will not say it is out of order, because I am linking up the thought in respect of a united Canada when I refer to the development which has taken place in Canada. The lack of a well-knit, harmonious economy, which I believe was hoped for but not attained at the time of confederation, has had a tendency to develop industrial central Canada, particularly the province of Ontario, at the expense of other sections of our country. During the past few years the citizens of all parts of Canada have come to understand that the prosperity of one section of our country is so interwoven with that of the other sections that our economic structure must be so shaped as to develop a closely knit and well-balanced economy which will develop and benefit all. That is understood to a greater extent than ever before. I was very pleased to listen to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Winters), that great Nova Scotian who has recently taken his place in the cabinet. When I say that, I am not for the moment thinking along political lines. Since this is the first opportunity I have had I am paying my respects to the choice made by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) in selecting this fine type of Nova Scotian to represent our province in the cabinet. I was very happy when I heard him expound his plans and hopes for a large building development that would not only take in his own province but reach from the Atlantic to the Pacific-plans which would produce houses for all Canadians. I think that is the right view to take. I do not want anything to happen, such as might happen if this motion were adopted, to divide one part of Canada from the other.
I was also pleased when the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) a month or so ago outlined plans which he had in mind to develop industry throughout the country instead of having it confined to a very large extent to the two provinces of Quebec and Ontario. I feel that the economy of our country can best be served if we decentralize industry. Our economy must be so built up that we shall have sufficient employment in the various sections of our country to keep all parts prosperous.
Because of this awakened interest in the industrial central sections, and the understanding shown by many of our leading citizens, I answer my first question as to whether Canada has real national status by saying that there is definite evidence that Canada has attained the status of nationhood.

Having reached that stage, it is only natural for the hon. member who introduced this motion to bring it forward in the hope of having a national anthem adopted by our country. I know that the great majority of hon. members are of the same mind as he is, that we should have a national anthem; but when he says "the national anthem" and defines what that national anthem is, then he is going to have a division of opinion. For that reason I repeat, it would be unwise to adopt the motion as it is at the present time.
Question.

Some hon. members are anxious to have the question put. It is unfortunate that after certain speakers have expressed their views others should not have the liberty that Canada enjoys today, and what we are so proud to brag about, namely, freedom of speech and opportunity for all.
A good speech.
Hon. members who have called "question" should be patient and permit other hon. members who want to take part in this debate to do so, and give them the same kind of hearing as they received.
Sing a few bars of "O Canada."

In reply to the interjection of the hon. member for Vancouver North, who is always interjecting in a humorous way, may I say to him that I feel quite sure he could do a very much better job of singing a few bars of "O Canada" than I can. If he likes to interject those remarks I have no objection whatsoever so long as he does not take up my time unnecessarily.
I was developing the thought that this country should be more closely united industrially and in other ways. I believe that in the feelings, interest, ideas and practices evolved from the Canadian environment and adapted to our needs and purposes this country is outstanding in two respects-in both good will and friendly disposition to all, both minorities and majorities alike.
I was surprised that hon. members should interrupt and call "question", as they did a moment ago. From all parts of Canada individuals and groups, as well as provincial leaders, representing widely varied opinions and interests, should co-operate to promote the recognition of Canada abroad to a greater extent even than at the present time.
With the background which I have just outlined, perhaps in a disjointed way, you will understand, Mr. Speaker, why I seek to emphasize that this is not an opportune time to press for the adoption of this motion.
Hear, hear.
Order.

I should thank the hon. members for appreciating the point which I have just made with regard to the outstanding position occupied by Canada. Today the proof of that fact is Canada's outstanding position in the international scene, the high regard for Canadian representatives, and the respect given and paid to Canada's new Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson).
Has that anything to do with the flag?

It has a definite connection with the flag because of the fact that Canada has attained a position which has made her the focus of the eyes of the world in her endeavours to maintain and perhaps lead other sections of the world in the movement for peace.
I believe you will understand me, Mr. Speaker, if I bring in the name of a great Nova Scotian, Joseph Howe, a man to whom we are largely indebted for responsible government in Nova Scotia. I was interested to note a short time ago that the legislature of Nova Scotia celebrated the anniversary of responsible government which took place, I believe, on March 11, 1848. That was when we had responsible government in Nova Scotia for the first time. Mr. Speaker, I am sure there are other members who would wish to take part in this debate.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Take your time.

I certainly do not wish to deprive them of the opportunity of contributing to the debate. I believe it can safely be said that the record of Canada stands as convincing proof that Canada is a nation which can make a great contribution to the community of nations. If that is so, then naturally we should have a national anthem and a flag of our own. I, for one, at the proper time would be happy to join with a majority in making a selection of a national anthem, but I should not like to see the selection narrowed down as we have it in the terms of this resolution, which states- That in the opinion of this house, the anthem "O Canada," in both the English and the French versions, should be the national anthem of this country.
I said the word "the" should be changed to "a", and that the matter should be laid over until a future date.
I believe I have covered those points I had intended to bring before the house. I consider this an important matter, and it would seem to me that the resolution is not worded as a majority of members would like to have
National Anthem
it. For that reason I sincerely trust no action will be taken in the matter at this time.
Mr. Speaker, I am in favour of the resolution as it stands.
Is it the intention of the hon. member to adjourn the debate?
Before doing so, do I understand that this honourable chamber is to proceed to the Senate immediately?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have to table some estimates.

I wish merely to move an amendment which I believe will be considered and accepted as a sincere effort to meet the wishes expressed by hon. members who have spoken this afternoon on the resolution before the house. Because I would like hon. members to express their views by their vote, I would move immediately, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair):
That after the word "country" at the end of the resolution the following words be added:
"as God Save the King is the anthem of all the nations of the commonwealth.
The resolution would then read:
That in the opinion of this house the anthem 'O Canada' in both the English and the French versions, should be the national anthem of this country, as 'God Save the King' is the anthem of all the nations of the commonwealth.
I would like to speak to the amendment, if I may.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
You will have lots of time.

Accordingly, the house went up to the Senate.
And having returned.

The Royal Assent

speechtext:
the adjournment of the house.
He said: Tomorrow we will take up the motion in the name of the Minister of Finance to go into ways and means.
The budget debate, in other words?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The budget debate.

speechtext: Next Tuesday, I believe.
Not until then?

speechtext:
On Friday we are taking up the supplementary estimates and at the moment I do not know whether we shall proceed on Friday night with it. Monday is private members' day, so I think the first occasion on which that motion could be considered would be on Tuesday.

Thursday, March 31, 1949
